newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's new finance minister a political veteran.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's new finance minister a political veteran.

text.p: Fifteen years after stepping down as South Korea's finance minister, political veteran Kang Kyung-shik has been summoned back for a repeat performance.
Those who know him say Kang is a reform-minded policy maker who will resist quick fixes for the struggling economy.
He is expected to draw from his nearly 30 years of political experience to help President Kim Young-sam make hard decisions.

Kang, 60, cut his teeth working on policy at the Economic Planning Board (EPB), the precursor to the Ministry of Finance and Economy. After 18 years at the bureau, he was tapped as minister of finance and economy by then-President Chun Doo Hwan.
During his 1982-1983 tenure, Kang left his mark as an aggressive reformist, who cared more for economic principles than politics, associates said.
He was an early advocate of a ban on the use of false names in financial transactions that camouflaged a huge underground economy.

"In the early '80s, he proposed the introduction of the real-name financial system, but failed due to strong pressure from groups with vested interests," said Yeo Kyung-ho, head of research at Daewoo Securities.
Disappointed by the failure, he left the civil service after a stint as Chun's presidential general secretary in 1983.
The real-name system was finally introduced by President Kim Young-sam in 1993.
In 1995 Kang was elected to the National Assembly as a member of the ruling New Korea Party.
Analysts hailed Kang's appointment, saying he would not shirk from making tough decisions.

"He proposed austerity programmes in the early 1980s," said Yeo. "At that time, most officials argued that they wanted to take growth-oriented policies, but he resisted that kind of pressure. He argued that we must take belt-tightening fiscal policies."
As finance minister, Kang argued for opening South Korea's markets to foreign competition. He also favoured the liberalisation of interest rates, economists said.
Kang's economic planning background also gave him a far wider perspective than other bureaucrats, analysts said.
"He has an overall view," said Shim Sang-dal, a former senior counsellor to the minister of finance.
But analysts were concerned that Kang's reform efforts would be stymied by election-year politics.
"In the current environment, restructuring is unlikely," said Richard Samuelson, head of research at SBC Warburg.

Kang was appointed in a reshuffle that saw seven ministerial portfolios change hands to help restore the president's image, badly damaged by the failure of Hanbo Steel Co under $5.8 billion in largely unsecured loans.
Opposition parties have accused the government of peddling influence to pressure banks into offering loans.
Kang is married with four children.
His chief of staff, Cha Sang-min, described him as an avid reader, who trolls through bookstores regularly to pick up new books from New Age science to history.
"He looks very conservative, but his mind is very liberal and he loves to tell jokes," Cha said.
